"Binita, I start in Bengaluru on the first of August. It's the fifth of June. I'm panicking."
"Leela, sit. Panic later. Paper first." Binita pulled a notebook across the dining table in their Lucknow flat. "What's the very first thing?"
"Notice period. Thirty days. I resign on Monday, the tenth."
"Next?"
"House. I'll fly down the weekend of the twenty-second to look."
"And Chintu's school?"
"Admissions there close mid-July. So I call three schools this week, apply by the thirtieth."
"Packers?"
"Book by the first of July. Moving day twenty-sixth."
"Bank, gas, Aadhaar address, his school records?"
"Last week of July, after the lease is signed."
Binita wrote each date down the left side. "Look. Eight weeks, one line each. That's not a disaster. That's a list."
Leela let out a long breath and ate a biscuit for the first time that evening.

When the Bengaluru transfer came through, I was sure I'd forget something. My daughter Riya was starting Class 2, and I'd never moved cities alone.
So on the first evening I opened a spreadsheet and broke the move into weeks.
Week 1: resign from the Lucknow branch, start my one-month notice. Week 2: call my future colleague Nikita for advice on areas. Week 3: fly down, see flats in HSR Layout and Koramangala. Week 4: apply to two schools, since admissions had a deadline. Week 5: book packers, confirm date. Week 6: lease signed, pay deposit. Week 7: move. Week 8: bank, gas, address changes, Riya's transfer certificate.
Things still went wrong. The packers came a day late. But because the school form had gone in during week four, Riya started on time.
The spreadsheet is still on my laptop. I opened it last week just to feel smug.
— Pooja

Relocation coordinator's note — Irfan, transfer from Jaipur to the Hyderabad office. Written by Noor.

Most transferees ask me for a list of "good areas" and sign the first lease a broker shows them. Irfan asked for three days' leave instead.
He arrived on a Thursday and did something simple: he travelled to our office from three different areas at peak hour. Gachibowli, Kondapur and Miyapur. He timed each trip on both mornings, eight-thirty and nine. He walked around each area in the evening, looked at the markets, checked where the nearest clinic was.
On Saturday he messaged me: "Kondapur looks fine online, but the morning traffic is forty-five minutes. Miyapur has the metro; it's thirty-five, reliable."
He signed a lease in Miyapur the following week.
What I did next: I've added a line to our relocation guide suggesting a peak-hour visit before signing.

Saturday night, Chennai

Came here for the weekend before the transfer starts next month. Dhruv let me stay on his sofa.
Online, Velachery looked perfect: cheaper rent, big malls, good reviews. So this morning at eight-forty-five I took the bus from Velachery to the office in Guindy. Fifty minutes, standing, in the heat. Tried it again at nine-thirty. Forty.
Then Dhruv drove me to Adyar and Nungambakkam. Walked around both in the afternoon. Adyar felt quiet, green, a proper vegetable market, and the train to Guindy took twenty minutes.
Online, I'd have signed for Velachery by now. In person, I'd hate that commute within a week.
Tomorrow I'm seeing two flats in Adyar. Rent is a little higher, but I'll get back an hour a day.
Glad I came instead of guessing.
— Thomas

subtype: Approach: negotiating a relocation package with the employer [Action]

Gautam, you're nervous about asking for more help with your transfer? Let me, Mahima, your old aunt, tell you about my first big move, from Kanpur to Mumbai, in 1998.
The bank offered me a promotion and a transfer, with two weeks to join. I was so happy I nearly said yes on the phone. But my father said, "Before you say yes, ask what they'll do to help you land."
So I wrote to the regional office. Three questions. Was there a relocation allowance? Could they give me temporary housing while I looked for a flat? Could I join in four weeks instead of two?
They said no to four weeks, but gave me three. And they put me in the bank's guest house in Chembur for a month, free.
That month saved me. I found a room near the station without panic. Ask, Gautam. The worst they say is no.

qa.a: In Chembur.

The offer email from the Gurgaon firm said Anjali had twenty-four hours to accept, and she was on a night bus back from her cousin's wedding in Jhansi.
At midnight, by the light of her phone, she typed a reply to Bhavna in HR. She kept it short: "I'm excited to accept. Before I confirm, may I ask three things? Is there a relocation allowance? Can the company offer temporary accommodation for my first few weeks? And could my joining date be the 15th rather than the 1st, so I can serve my notice?"
She hit send and dozed off against the window.
At seven, as the bus pulled into Delhi, Bhavna had replied. Joining on the 15th: fine. Relocation allowance: a fixed amount, as per policy. And a month in the company guest house near the office.
Anjali sent her acceptance from the bus stand, grinning, still in yesterday's clothes.

subtype: Approach: underestimating settling costs and time [Pitfall]

Jamal and Aiko landed in Toronto with their four-year-old in late January, sure they'd be settled in a week.
They weren't. The apartment needed a deposit of two months' rent up front, much more than they'd budgeted. The internet company's first appointment was in twelve days. The gas for the stove wasn't connected, so for the first week they ate cold sandwiches and takeaway, which cost a fortune.
Aiko spent her mornings on hold with utility companies. Jamal started his new job exhausted, checking the bank balance at every break. They had brought only a little cash, expecting to be earning by the second week, but the first paycheque didn't arrive until the end of the month.
One night, Aiko sat on an unopened box and said, "We planned the job. We didn't plan the landing."
Jamal didn't argue. He was thinking the same thing.

qa.a: Twelve days.

qa.a: Aiko felt exhausted and stressed, realising they had planned for the job but not for settling in.

qa.a: They could have asked people who'd moved there about deposits and setup times, and brought more money for the first month.

Joseph had driven a delivery van in Thodupuzha for five years when an electronics factory in Hosur offered him a supervisor's job with much higher pay.
"Take it," his friend Kishore said. "That money! You'll be rich."
Joseph did the sum in his head: the new salary minus the old. He signed without asking anything else.
In Hosur, rooms near the factory were taken, so he rented one in a town forty minutes away, at twice his old rent. The factory bus left at six. His wife and daughter stayed back in Thodupuzha until the school year ended, so he also paid for trips home every other weekend.
By the third month, he sat down with a notebook. After rent, bus, meals and train tickets, he had only slightly more than before. And he saw his daughter four days a month.
He called Kishore that night. "The number was big. The life is small."

Hansa, you've just moved to Delhi and you sound lonely on the phone. Let me, Zainab, your Phuppo, tell you what I did when I moved to Hyderabad for my first job in 1995.
Everyone warned me the first months in a new city are the loneliest. So I didn't wait for friends to find me.
In the very first week, I joined the evening Urdu poetry circle at the library near my hostel. I was terrible at reciting, but it gave me somewhere to be on Thursdays.
The same week, I wrote a letter to Shabnam, my college roommate, who lived in Secunderabad. She came on Sunday with biryani.
I asked the older women in the hostel which lady doctor they trusted, and which kirana shop gave fair weights. I had both names written in my diary by the end of the month.
When I got fever that winter, I wasn't alone. That's the whole secret, Hansa. Build the net before you fall.

Sunday, Nashik

The movers come on Thursday. Tonight Minakshi and I sat on the floor among the boxes and did the "what if it goes wrong" list.
What if the new job in Bengaluru isn't what they promised? It happens. My cousin quit after two months.
So:
1. We've set aside three months of our expenses in a separate account, not to be touched unless we need it.
2. We're keeping this flat for one more month. The landlord agreed. If things go badly in the first weeks, there's somewhere to come back to.
3. Backup: my old manager said I could return to a similar role here, or I can take up the Pune offer I turned down, if they still need someone.
Minakshi said, "So it's a door, not a wall." Exactly. We can walk back through it if we have to.
Strangely, now I'm more excited than scared.
— Lokesh

Chetan had signed a lease in Thane before the monsoon, when the drive to his new office in Andheri looked fine on a map.
By July, it wasn't fine. Flooded roads turned the commute into two and a half hours each way. He left at seven and got home at ten. He fell asleep on the sofa most nights in his office clothes.
His colleague Divyansh finally said, "You look like a ghost. Why not move closer?"
"The lease has a three-month penalty."
"And how much are you losing in sleep?"
That weekend Chetan did the sums and thought it through. He'd picked Thane from photos and a Sunday visit, not from a single weekday commute in the rain. It wasn't a stupid choice, just one made with too little information.
He paid the penalty and moved to a smaller flat in Andheri East, twelve minutes from work. The first night he slept eight hours straight.

Sameer had a transfer letter to Bengaluru and a list of questions he couldn't answer. So on Wednesday he took two colleagues out for lunch near the Noida office: Noor, who had moved to Bengaluru and back, and Indu, who had moved to Chennai with two children.
"Broker fees," Noor said first. "In some areas it's a full month's rent. Ask before you visit anything."
"School admissions," Indu said. "They close much earlier than you think. For my son's school, it was January, not April."
"And avoid the area near the airport road if you work in the south," Noor added. "The traffic will eat your life."
Sameer wrote everything down. He'd planned to arrive in April and look for schools then. He'd planned to use whatever broker the first website suggested.
On the drive back, he did the sums in his head. Two mistakes avoided, just from one lunch.

qa.q: When did school admissions close for Indu's son's school?
qa.a: In January, not April.

qa.q: How did Sameer feel on the drive back?
qa.a: Sameer felt relieved and grateful, realising one lunch had saved him from two costly mistakes.

qa.q: What else could Sameer do with the advice he received?
qa.a: He could apply to schools right away and ask for broker fees in writing before visiting any flats.

qa.q: How might Noor and Indu feel about sharing their experience?
qa.a: They likely felt useful and pleased to help, turning their own hard lessons into advice for a colleague.

grounding: It shows someone talking to two colleagues who relocated earlier and learning about broker fees, school timelines and areas to avoid, saving him from mistakes.

subtype: Approach: asking colleagues who moved before for advice [Thinking]
passage:
"Rafiq, you moved to Mumbai two years ago, right? Can I ask you some stupid questions?"
"No stupid questions, Jatin. Sit. Lata moved last year too; she's coming."
"Okay. First: brokers. What should I expect?"
"In some areas they charge a full month's rent," Rafiq said. "Negotiate before you see anything, not after."
Lata sat down with her tea. "And schools. Is your daughter joining Class 1?"
"Yes, in June."
"Then you're already late. Most schools there close admissions by February. Call this week."
Jatin stopped writing. "I thought I'd look after I moved."
"That's what I thought too," Lata said. "My son lost a year of choices."
"Last one," Rafiq said. "Don't take a flat on the far side of the creek if you work in Lower Parel. It looks close on a map. It isn't."
Jatin looked at his notes. "You've just saved me a year of mistakes."

qa.q: By when do most schools close admissions, according to Lata?
qa.a: By February.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel when he stopped writing?
qa.a: Jatin felt shocked and a little alarmed, realising the plan to look for schools after moving would have been too late.

qa.q: What else could Jatin do with this advice right away?
qa.a: Jatin could call schools this week and set a rule to agree broker fees before visiting any flat.

qa.q: How might Lata feel sharing her son's experience?
qa.a: Lata may feel a little regretful about her own mistake but glad to spare Jatin's daughter the same loss.

grounding: It shows someone asking two colleagues who relocated earlier and learning about broker fees, school admission timelines and areas to avoid, saving him from costly mistakes.
